Occupational mobility tends to decline with age, but age is a proxy for
the underlying mechanism rather than the mechanism itself.
@mincer1981labor show empirically that age effects on mobility largely
disappear once tenure is controlled, and attribute the residual to
specific human capital accumulation rather than aging per se: as workers
commit to an occupational path, the wedge between their current wage and
outside options widens, making mobility increasingly costly. Tenure is
their operational measure of that wedge, but the wedge is unobservable
in principle, what they estimate is the hazard of separation as a
function of job duration, not specific capital directly. OES approaches
the same underlying quantity from the supply side: rather than inferring
specific capital from the duration of job spells, it reads off the
credential selectivity of the occupation from the equilibrium education
mix. A newly trained and a 20-year veteran physician occupy the same
high-OES occupation, and should be similarly immobile; a newly appointed
and a long-tenured senior manager occupy the same low-OES occupation and
should remain similarly mobile. Tenure varies within each pair but the
mobility prediction does not, because what constrains mobility is the
credential selectivity of the occupation, not the worker's time in it.
This is a distinction tenure cannot identify as a stable property of the
occupation, but OES can.

## Cost Metrics {#sec-cost-metrics}

The skill distance matrix $C_{\text{skill}}$ is constructed from 161 
O\*NET measures spanning skills, abilities, knowledge, and work 
activities, mapped to NOC 2021 occupations via a purpose-built 
crosswalk @onet_to_noc. An alternative approach would be to 
use OaSIS occupation-level skill profiles, but we construct our own 
crosswalk for a specific reason: falsifiability. The horse race 
requires that measurement error in the skill distance matrix be 
attributable to a known source: imprecision in the O\*NET 
to NOC 2021 mapping. OaSIS obscures the structure of that mapping, making 
it impossible to characterize where and how measurement error enters 
$C_{\text{skill}}$; our crosswalk makes this structure transparent 
and therefore makes the identification strategy falsifiable. Each NOC 
is represented as a weighted average of its constituent O\*NET 
occupations, with weights determined by the crosswalk mapping.  For more details on the mapping see Appendix A.

O\*NET provides two scales for each measure: Importance (how important the attribute is to the occupation) and Level (the degree to which the attribute is required). Both scales are standardized to a common 0--10 range and combined via geometric mean, yielding a single score that reflects both the relevance and the intensity of each attribute. The geometric mean is preferred over the arithmetic mean as it penalizes cases where one scale is near zero, an attribute that is important but required at negligible level, or required at high level but deemed unimportant, receives a lower composite score than one scoring moderately on both dimensions. The two scales are highly correlated ($\rho=.96$), so this choice is unlikely to be consequential for the resulting distance matrix but we note it for transparency.

The 161 O\*NET skill items are correlated, so raw Euclidean distance in the full item space implicitly upweights dimensions measured by many items over those measured by few. We apply PCA to the standardised profiles to remove this redundancy, then retain the number of components needed to preserve pairwise distance rank ordering: starting from $k = 1$, we increment until the Spearman rank correlation between pairwise distances in the $k$-dimensional PCA space and in the full 161-dimensional space exceeds 0.99. This criterion, rank preservation rather than variance explained, is chosen because the object of interest is the distance matrix itself, not the underlying skill dimensions. Twelve components satisfy it. The skill distance between any two occupations is then the Euclidean distance between their coordinates in this 12-dimensional space. An interactive heatmap of the resulting distance matrix is available in the [online companion.](https://rpmartin.github.io/not-one-thing-companion/#sec-skill-heatmap)

A small number of off-diagonal cells of $C_{\text{skill}}$ are exactly zero, because a few NOC unit groups map to the same O\*NET occupation: NOC resolves distinctions that O\*NET does not, so occupations O\*NET treats as one are assigned identical skill profiles and zero mutual skill distance. This affects 280 of the roughly 253,000 ordered off-diagonal pairs (0.11\%), falling into 36 groups of mutually skill-identical occupations. The zeros are not measurement error: where O\*NET does not separate two occupations, no O\*NET-based skill measure can, and zero distance is the correct statement of that limit. We keep them, and characterize the groups in Appendix A.

The binary switching cost matrix $C_{\text{binary}}$ assigns a cost of zero to remaining in the same occupation and one to any transition. Under entropically regularized optimal transport, this implies that all off-diagonal transitions share the same switching cost, so conditional on leaving an occupation, relative transition probabilities are governed entirely by the destination scaling factors, which are pinned by the destination margins. In other words, the origin occupation provides no additional information for ordering alternative destinations once a move occurs.

$C_{\text{binary}}$ serves two roles in the analysis. First, it is the theoretical straw man in the global horse race: the hypothesis that mobility costs depend only on whether a switch occurs rather than on where it leads. If this hypothesis holds, $C_{\text{binary}}$ should rationalize observed mobility better than either $C_{\text{skill}}$ or $C_{\text{hierarchy}}$. Second, $C_{\text{binary}}$ is a plausible description of labour markets in which occupational distance carries little information about the destinations of movers. In such settings, conditioning on a move, destinations are allocated according to the destination scalings, which track overall prevalence rather than proximity to the origin occupation, so the additional geometry imposed by the structured metrics does not improve predictive performance.

The horse race therefore turns on destination structure rather than mobility rates, since all three metrics accommodate the observed propensity to remain in the same occupation. This second role motivates the Binary sub-regime hypothesis: where human capital is sufficiently specific that occupational distance does not systematically order exits, binary is not merely a degenerate benchmark but a substantive model of mobility. Because it imposes no origin-specific structure on off-diagonal transitions, its only free mechanism is the aggregate stay--move split, governed by the single parameter $\varepsilon$, which sets the overall degree of mobility. @sec-local uses this characterization when comparing where the three metrics peak.

The hierarchical distance matrix $C_{\text{hierarchy}}$ is derived directly from the NOC 2021 taxonomy, treating the occupational classification structure as a tree metric. Distance between any two occupations is defined as follows: zero if all five digits match (same unit group); one if the first four digits match (same minor group, different unit group); two if the first three digits match (same sub-major group, different minor group); three plus the absolute difference in TEER level if only the first digit matches (same broad occupational category, different sub-major group); and nine for any cross-category transition. The absolute TEER difference ranges from zero to five, so within-category distances range from three to eight, preserving a strict separation from the cross-category sentinel value of nine.  An interactive hierarchical distance heatmap of the resulting matrix is available in the [online companion.](https://rpmartin.github.io/not-one-thing-companion/#sec-hier-heatmap)

Occupation broad groups function as silos (bounded mobility clusters with limited entry points and internal progression along skill levels [@doeringer1971internal]), and TEER levels function as platforms within each silo, capturing the vertical skill stratification that governs upward movement. By construction, any between-platform move (minimum distance 4) is further than any within-platform move (maximum distance 3), and any cross-silo move (distance 9) is further than any within-silo move (maximum distance 8). The occupation broad group is a coarser unit than the occupational clusters described by @althauser1989, but the appropriate level of aggregation for the horse race: a finer partition would increase the preponderance of cross-category sentinel values in the hierarchical distance distribution, collapsing the metric's geometry toward binary and undermining its role as a distinct candidate in the horse race.

## Cost Metric Normalization

The three cost matrices are defined on different scales by construction: skill 
distances are continuous and spread over a wide range, hierarchical distances 
are discrete with a sentinel value of nine reserved for cross-category 
transitions, and binary distances take only the values zero and one. Because 
the cost matrix scale and $\varepsilon$ are not separately identified, the 
choice of anchor shifts where a metric's peak falls on the $\varepsilon$ axis 
but not the peak fit it attains; the winning metric is therefore invariant to 
normalization. Normalization matters instead for the legibility of the sweep 
plots: on a common $\varepsilon$ grid, matrices on different scales imply 
different effective $\varepsilon$, so the curves are not visually comparable 
unless first placed on a common scale. For the same reason we anchor at a 
substantively meaningful unit, so that position on the $\varepsilon$ axis 
remains interpretable.

We normalize skill and hierarchical distances to a common scale by anchoring 
both at a meaningful unit of hierarchical distance: distance 3, the maximum 
distance without changing platforms. Distance 3 falls at the fourth percentile 
of the hierarchical distribution, reflecting the preponderance of cross-silo 
pairs. The corresponding fourth percentile of the skill distance distribution 
is 7.145. Dividing hierarchical distances by 3 and skill distances by 7.145 
anchors both matrices at the same point in their respective distributions. 
Binary distances are not subject to this anchoring; their two-point support is 
shown for reference. @fig-cdfs gives the empirical CDFs before and after 
normalization. Normalization pins the skill and hierarchical distributions to 
the same point at the anchor, but their shapes remain distinct: hierarchical 
distance is discrete, with the small minority of within-platform pairs spread 
below the anchor and the bulk of pairs concentrated at the cross-category 
sentinel, while skill distance is continuous and dispersed across a wider 
range. This residual difference in shape is the separability the horse race 
exploits; normalization equalizes scale, not geometry.


```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-cdfs
#| fig-cap: "Empirical CDFs of the three cost matrices before and after normalization; normalization places skill and hierarchical on a common scale for the shared $\\varepsilon$ sweeps without equalizing their shape."
cdfs
```

## Mobility Data {#sec-data}

The analysis uses the Census 2016--2021 longitudinal file, constructed 
by linking long-form respondents across the two census cycles via the 
Derived Record Depository (DRD), Statistics Canada's national 
longitudinal database of personal identifiers. Linkage is 
probabilistic; details of the matching keys and overall linkage rate 
will be verified upon data access.

[Linkage Details Here]

In the following analysis we make use of a \emph{measurement complete} 
subset of the linked data where we observe occupation, field of study, 
highest educational attainment, class of worker and age in both 2016 and 2021.

[Missingness Details Here]

Canada's NOC 2021 hierarchy nominally contains 516 unit groups, but 
the five Senior Manager NOCs (00011--00015) are aggregated into NOC 
00018 in the CIP-NOC table used to derive the specificity constructs, leaving 512 
occupations. Eight unit groups have no admissible O*NET mapping and 
are excluded from all estimation samples, leaving 504 occupations in 
the analysis.

These 504 occupations are the universe over which the sub-regime
partition is defined: the OES ranking that fixes the three sub-regimes
`r format_counts(teer_counts)` is computed over all 504, and
@tbl-partition-crosstab and @fig-regimes are likewise on the full 504.
The mapping-quality exclusion enters one step later, at estimation
rather than partition. <!-- REVIEW #1: state the base the decile is computed on. The 8 no-O*NET-mapping exclusions and the 50 bottom-decile-mapped occupations must be disjoint sets for 504 - 50 = 454 to hold as written. If the H×SS composite is scored after the 8 are already dropped, the decile is of ~504 (giving ~50), say so explicitly. If it is scored on 512, the arithmetic and the disjointness both need restating. A referee will check 516 - 4 - 8 = 504 and then ask where the 50 come from. -->
The bottom decile of the $H \times SS$ mapping
quality composite (Appendix A) flags 50 poorly mapped occupations, and
the local clean and non-local clean samples are built from transitions
among the remaining 454. A transition is dropped whenever either
endpoint is one of the 50, so the clean estimation samples run on the
454 cleanly mapped occupations while the partition they inherit was
cut on the full 504.

There are two core subsamples used in both the local and non-local mobility analyses. Their role reverses depending on whether they serve as the primary identification sample or the falsification sample. The two samples are separated by the size of the human-capital increment a worker acquires between 2016 and 2021, as developed in @sec-rp. We operationalise the increment from the education record, the cross product of highest attainment and field of study, using the field-of-study classification's two-digit series as the unit of field distance.\[To be determined whether CIP in the linked file is harmonized or versioned.\] A worker brings a large increment into play by reaching a higher level of attainment, or by changing field at the same level across two-digit series, which is retraining into an area where the original credential does not transfer. A change in the recorded education between cycles is read as specific human capital becoming operative within the window, whether freshly earned or earned earlier and only now put to use, since the record dates neither. A worker whose education changes only within a two-digit series at the same level brings a small increment into play and is grouped with those with no change: these same level, same 2 digit CIP new attainments make up X% of all new attainments.

The \emph{local clean sample} comprises individuals whose education increment is small by this criterion, with no self-employment and an O*NET-to-NOC mapping quality score above the bottom decile. This is the sample where distance-based models should best rationalise mobility: no specific human capital becomes newly operative over the inter-census period, so the 2016 occupation is an informative anchor. Any education already in place is reflected in where the worker starts and, so long as it is not newly brought to bear, does not drive subsequent movement.

The \emph{non-local clean sample} comprises individuals whose education increment is large by this criterion, subject to the same measurement restrictions as the local clean sample. This is the sample where the specificity regression should have the best fit: a large increment may open a wormhole to a distant occupation, the 2016 occupation is no longer an informative anchor, and specific human capital becoming operative within the inter-census window is the active ingredient in long-distance jumps. In contrast, the local model will struggle to rationalize these transitions on the basis of distance.

In addition, for both models we investigate the effect of measurement error in occupation, when the data is otherwise appropriate for the model being fit. We treat occupation measurement error as likely when individuals are self-employed: self-employed workers frequently perform multiple roles simultaneously, making a single occupation an unreliable summary of their occupational position. We do not treat an inconsistency between reported occupation and reported attainment as measurement error. Under the latent--operative distinction developed in @sec-rp, such an inconsistency is more naturally read as an activation lag, a credential held but not yet operative at the 2016 reference week, or newly operative and not yet reflected in the 2021 occupation, than as a misreported occupation. This is signal, not noise: the 2016 case is precisely the dormant credential the reinstatement of @sec-AD recovers, and the 2021 case is a genuine in-scope increment whose destination the reference week has not yet caught. Screening these cases as mismeasured would delete the very phenomenon the partition is built to study. We rely instead on the accuracy of the census occupation coding itself, Statistics Canada's flagship instrument, for which the assumption that a reported NOC is a genuine labour-market outcome rather than a coding error is well founded; residual miscoding is second-order relative to activation lag and enters distance measurement as symmetric attenuating noise.

For non-local mobility we can perform one further diagnostic: the effect of poor skill mapping from O\*NET to NOC, when the data is otherwise appropriate for the model being fit. Poor skill mapping is identified by the bottom decile of the O\*NET-to-NOC mapping quality composite. Poor mapping introduces noise specifically into $C_{\text{skill}}$ while leaving 
$C_{\text{hierarchy}}$ unaffected, a metric-specific prediction 
that serves as a falsification of the mapping quality composite 
itself. This diagnostic is not available for local mobility. As noted
above, the local clean subset is built from transitions among the 454
cleanly mapped occupations, whereas the mapping quality subset is built
from transitions involving at least one of the 50 poorly mapped
occupations, so the two subsets have disjoint cells by construction.
Since $\Delta KL$ and $\Delta CWTVD$ require a common set of possible origin-destination pairs to be comparable, no valid comparison is possible between the local clean and mapping quality subsets.

## Local Model {#sec-local}

Mobility costs are latent: workers' switching costs are not observable 
in principle, so any distance matrix is necessarily a specification of 
an unobservable quantity. The three candidate matrices, skill, 
hierarchical, and binary, represent distinct hypotheses about the 
structure of those latent costs.

The entropy-regularized optimal transport problem minimizes the following Lagrangian, where the first term is the transport cost, the second is the entropic regularization penalizing deterministic transport plans, and the third and fourth enforce the marginal constraints $\sum_j P_{ij} = a_i$ and $\sum_i P_{ij} = b_j$ via dual variables $f_i$ and
$g_j$.

$$\mathcal{L} = \sum_{ij} P_{ij} C_{ij} + \varepsilon \sum_{ij} P_{ij}(\log P_{ij} - 1) + \sum_i f_i(a_i - \sum_j P_{ij}) + \sum_j g_j(b_j - \sum_i P_{ij})$$

where $a_i$ and $b_j$ are the empirical marginal distributions in 2016 and 2021 respectively. 

The first-order conditions yield:
\begin{equation}
\log P_{ij} = \frac{f_i}{\varepsilon} + \frac{g_j}{\varepsilon} - 
\frac{C_{ij}}{\varepsilon}
\end{equation}
Exponentiating, the optimal transport plan takes the form 
$P^\star_{ij} = u_i \, e^{-C_{ij}/\varepsilon} \, v_j$, where 
$u_i = e^{f_i/\varepsilon}$ and $v_j = e^{g_j/\varepsilon}$ are 
scaling vectors. Strict convexity of the regularized objective 
guarantees a unique solution. The solution is therefore a row- and 
column-rescaling of the exponential kernel $K_{ij} = e^{-C_{ij}/\varepsilon}$, where the Sinkhorn algorithm recovers it by alternating row and column 
normalization until both marginal constraints are satisfied to within a specified tolerance. All computations use a log-domain Sinkhorn solver 
for numerical stability, implemented in the \texttt{safesink} R package [@safesink].

In log space, the optimal transport plan decomposes into additive origin effects
($\log u_i$), additive destination effects ($\log v_j$), and a dyadic cost term
($-C_{ij}/\varepsilon$). The scaling vectors correspond to Lagrange multipliers on
the marginal constraints and adjust to ensure the implied joint distribution matches
the observed origin and destination occupation stocks, absorbing any components of
the data that operate at the level of origins or destinations alone given the
specified cost structure. The cost matrix captures the residual structure that
depends on origin--destination pairing. The horse race asks which specification of
that dyadic structure best rationalizes observed transitions.

The gravity model [@anderson_vanwincoop_2003; @silva2006log] estimates origin and destination fixed effects jointly with the cost parameters, and that joint estimation is precisely the problem in our setting. Because the fixed effects are fit to the transitions, they carry the slack to absorb variation that a wrong cost matrix leaves misfit, so a misspecified geometry achieves good fit by compensating through them rather than by being right. Using a gravity model would be akin to giving the slower horses performance-enhancing drugs in inverse proportion to their natural speed: the race is closer than it should be, and the finishing order may be perturbed. EROT fixes the margins at observed values, and its scaling vectors are pinned to those margins rather than fit to the cells, so they cannot take up a wrong geometry's misfit. Each cost matrix must earn its fit in the residual dyadic structure, with no compensation for its own misspecification, which separates the question of where mobility flows, shaped by the cost matrix and the focus of this paper, from the question of why workers move. Wages, amenities, and other occupation-level incentives operate through the margins and are deliberately outside the scope of the identification strategy.

One might ask why we do not simply run PPML with the margins constrained to their observed values, since EROT and the gravity model share the functional form $u_i \, e^{-C_{ij}/\varepsilon} \, v_j$: the entropic plan is Anderson--van Wincoop gravity with $\beta = -1/\varepsilon$ and the scaling vectors in the role of the fixed effects. The constraint is not an extra step, because PPML with a full set of origin and destination fixed effects already reproduces the observed margins at its optimum; the first-order conditions for the fixed effects are the margin-matching equations. What the referee's constrained regression would still do, and EROT would not, is estimate a separate distance coefficient $\beta$ per cost matrix, jointly with the fixed effects, so that a misspecified geometry can shrink its own $\beta$ toward zero while the fixed effects absorb the misfit, leaving a coefficient that cannot distinguish a geometry that does not order destinations from one that does but was rescued at the margins. EROT removes exactly that freedom: it pins $\beta = -1/\varepsilon$ on a grid common to every metric, so no candidate estimates its own distance-sensitivity; it scores the constructed plan against the observed off-diagonal cells rather than maximising the plan's own likelihood, which is what lets the geometry-aware $\Delta CWTVD$ criterion enter at all, a criterion PPML's likelihood has no analogue for; and it imposes the margins unconditionally, for every $C$ and every $\varepsilon$, rather than achieving them at a jointly fitted optimum, so margin-matching is orthogonal to the geometry question rather than co-solved with it. Constrained PPML with those three defects repaired is not an alternative to the entropic transport formulation; it is that formulation.

The fairness of the race has a second aspect that distinguishes it from
an in-sample regression fit. A cost matrix is fixed a priori, not
estimated from the transitions, and given the margins and a value of
$\varepsilon$ the transport plan is then fully determined. The plan is a
prediction of the off-diagonal transition structure that never consults
that structure: nothing in its construction is chosen by looking at where
workers actually moved, so a metric that fits the observed transitions
well has not earned the fit by bending toward the data the way a regression
with enough parameters does. It committed to a geometry in advance and the
geometry happened to order destinations the way workers moved. Good fit is
therefore not cheap here in the way good in-sample fit is cheap in
regression, and the usual worry about overfitting the outcome does not
arise, because the outcome was not fit. The one degree of freedom is
$\varepsilon$, a single scale parameter swept over a grid and common to
every metric, so no candidate is granted more flexibility than another.
The diagonal is the one place all metrics coincide regardless of geometry:
every cost matrix assigns zero self-distance, $C_{ii}=0$, so every plan
concentrates mass on the diagonal and reproduces the aggregate stay/move
split. That shared diagonal credit is common ground rather than a
discriminating signal, and the race is decided on the off-diagonal
allocation, which is exactly the part no cost matrix was allowed to see.




The regularization parameter $\varepsilon$ has a natural interpretation
in the random utility framework. The optimal transport plan $P^\star_{ij} = u_i \, e^{-C_{ij}/\varepsilon} \, v_j$ is the static equilibrium of a discrete choice model in which workers draw idiosyncratic utility shocks scaled by $\varepsilon$ over destination occupations. Low values of $\varepsilon$ concentrate the transport plan on cost-minimizing assignments, approaching a deterministic reallocation in the limit; high values diffuse mobility across destinations, approaching the independence baseline $P_{ij} = a_i b_j$ as $\varepsilon \to \infty$. The RUM analogy governs the interior structure of the transport plan, how probability mass is allocated across origin-destination pairs, but does not extend to the margins. In a standard logit model the choice probabilities are outcomes of utility maximization with no constraint on their aggregates; in EROT the origin and destination occupation distributions are hard constraints that the transport plan must exactly reproduce. This distinction is methodologically consequential: because the margins cannot adjust to absorb cost misspecification, a poorly chosen cost matrix cannot hide behind fixed effects or scale recalibration, its misfit appears directly in the objective. 

A critical identification constraint follows directly from the form of 
the optimal transport plan: only the ratio $C_{ij}/\varepsilon$ enters 
$P^\star$. The scale of the cost matrix and the value of $\varepsilon$ 
are therefore not separately identified, and results reported at a 
single value of $\varepsilon$ are uninterpretable without an implicit 
normalization assumption. We evaluate across a wide log-spaced grid of 
$\varepsilon$ values from 0.1 to 1000, deliberately broader than the range 
expected to be informative, to ensure the informative region is fully 
contained within the evaluated range and its boundaries are visually apparent.

The horse race is evaluated using two complementary fit metrics, both
normalized relative to the independence baseline $P^{\text{ind}}_{ij} =
a_i b_j$, so that 0 indicates no improvement over independence, 1
indicates perfect fit, and negative values indicate a transport plan that fits observed mobility worse than independence. 

The first metric is relative KL divergence improvement:

$$\Delta KL = \frac{KL(P^{\text{obs}} \parallel P^{\text{ind}}) - KL(P^{\text{obs}} \parallel \hat{P})}{KL(P^{\text{obs}} \parallel P^{\text{ind}})}$$

where $KL(P \parallel Q) = \sum_{ij} P_{ij} \log(P_{ij} / Q_{ij})$.
This measures the share of the divergence between observed transitions
and independence that is explained by the fitted transport plan. KL
divergence is sensitive to probability mass wherever it is misallocated, but is geometry-blind: misallocating mass to a nearby occupation is penalized identically to misallocating it to a distant one.

The second metric is relative Cost-Weighted Total Variation Distance (CWTVD) improvement:

$$\Delta CWTVD = \frac{CWTVD(P^{\text{obs}}, P^{\text{ind}}) - CWTVD(P^{\text{obs}}, \hat{P})}{CWTVD(P^{\text{obs}}, P^{\text{ind}})}$$

where $CWTVD(P^{\text{obs}}, \hat{P}) = \sum_{ij}
\frac{|P^{\text{obs}}_{ij} - \hat{P}_{ij}|}{2} \cdot C_{ij}$. 

CWTVD is a cost-weighted extension of total variation distance: the 
classical TVD between discrete distributions, 
$\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ij}|P_{ij} - Q_{ij}|$, is extended by weighting 
each absolute residual by the corresponding entry of a cost matrix, 
penalizing probability mass misallocated to geometrically distant 
origin-destination pairs more heavily than mass misallocated to nearby 
ones. The cost matrix $C$ that weights the CWTVD residuals is not fixed to a single blend. For adjudication we score $\Delta CWTVD$ under each of the two informative cost matrices in turn, $C_{\text{skill}}$ and $C_{\text{hierarchy}}$, treating each as sole judge. These two are the endpoints of the family of blends the score could use: because $C_{\text{binary}}$ is flat off-diagonal and contributes no off-diagonal weighting, that family is the convex hull of $C_{\text{skill}}$ and $C_{\text{hierarchy}}$, and a metric that leads at both endpoints leads under every blend between them. Scoring at the two endpoints therefore certifies geometric soundness across the whole family, where a single blended judge would certify it only at one interior point. The two informative matrices are genuinely separable: the cell-level correlation between $C_{\text{skill}}$ and $C_{\text{hierarchy}}$ is about 0.3, so the endpoints are far enough apart to bracket a real interval rather than two near-identical judges.

We adjudicate the horse race on the likelihood criterion and the
geometry-aware criterion, the latter evaluated at both informative
endpoints, and a metric wins only by leading on all of them. The
likelihood criterion is peak relative KL improvement. For each
candidate cost matrix we maximise $\Delta KL$ over the $\varepsilon$
grid, and the reason for using it is that the EROT plan
$P^\star_{ij} = u_i\, e^{-C_{ij}/\varepsilon}\, v_j$ is the equilibrium of
a multinomial-logit discrete-choice model. Comparing candidates by their
maximised likelihood is then identical to comparing their peak relative
KL improvement, so peak $\Delta KL$ is maximum-likelihood model
selection rather than a fit heuristic. The geometry-aware criterion is
peak relative CWTVD improvement over the same grid, scored under each
informative judge, $C_{\text{skill}}$ and $C_{\text{hierarchy}}$, in
turn. KL is blind to the geometry of the outcome space, scoring a unit
of misallocated mass the same whether it lands on a near pair or a far
one. CWTVD weights each misallocation by distance, and across mixed
data-generating processes it separates the two correlated informative
geometries, $\mathrm{corr}(C_{\mathrm{skill}}, C_{\mathrm{hierarchy}}) =
0.3$, more sharply than KL does, with the gap between them tracking how
far the true mixture sits from balance. The [online companion](https://rpmartin.github.io/not-one-thing-companion) documents this directly.
 
The two justifications are independent. KL carries the likelihood
interpretation but cannot see geometry; CWTVD sees geometry but carries no
likelihood interpretation. Neither contains the other, so we hold them on
equal footing rather than naming one primary, and a win must satisfy the
likelihood criterion and the geometry-aware criterion at both endpoints.

The exclusion of recorded decreases (@sec-rp) enters the horse race with a
direction we state in advance. A decrease is an unpredictable career change,
which fits the Binary metric and misfits the two structured metrics, so
retaining decreases would raise Binary's peak and lower the others'. Excluding
them is therefore conservative in the Binary sub-regime, where it removes
observations that support the hypothesised winner, and flattering in the Skill
and Hierarchy sub-regimes, where it removes observations that misfit the
hypothesised winner. Because the exclusion helps us in two of the three
sub-regimes, we report the horse race both ways at the primary OES partition:
the winning metric and its peak improvement with decreases excluded, our
primary specification, and with decreases retained. The exclusion is on a
pre-outcome membership rule, a recorded level decrease, applied uniformly and
without reference to fit, so the comparison is a check rather than a choice; we
pre-commit to the prediction that the winner is unchanged in every sub-regime,
that Binary's peak rises modestly under retention, and that the structured
metrics' peaks fall modestly, each by the signed amount the career-change
reading implies. A winner that survived retention despite the misfit it adds in
the Skill and Hierarchy sub-regimes is not an artifact of the exclusion.
 
The case for CWTVD differs from the case for KL in what the estimation data
can and cannot show. The
resolving-power property is established under known data-generating
processes, as one establishes consistency or test power for an estimator
rather than reading it off the sample the estimator is later applied to.
It can be established only that way. The property is a claim about the
mapping from a known true mixture to the gap CWTVD reports between metrics,
and checking that mapping requires holding the truth fixed and reading off
the measurement, which presupposes knowing the truth. The estimation
sample is a single transition matrix drawn from one unknown mixture, so it
yields one gap and no reference mixture against which that gap's size could
be judged. No quantity in this sample, or in any single observed labour
market, can confirm or disconfirm the property. The simulation is not
preliminary evidence awaiting empirical confirmation but the only support
the claim admits. The simulation validates the instrument and the
estimation sample takes the measurement, and we make no prediction that
the Canadian data will confirm CWTVD's advantage. The data answers a
different question, which geometry governs Canadian mobility, and the
resolving-power property is what licenses trusting CWTVD's answer to that
question when it parts from KL's.
 
We compare peaks rather than improvement at any single $\varepsilon$
because of the same non-identification that motivated the grid above:
only the ratio $C_{ij}/\varepsilon$ enters $P^\star$, so a metric's
improvement at a fixed $\varepsilon$ has no interpretation without an
implicit normalization, and the peak is the scale-free summary that
removes the ambiguity. Each candidate traces an
interior maximum over the grid: at low $\varepsilon$ the plan
over-concentrates on the diagonal relative to the observed move rate, and
as $\varepsilon \to \infty$ it diffuses to the independence baseline
$P_{ij} = a_i b_j$, where improvement returns to zero. The grid from $0.1$
to $1000$ is wide enough that all three candidates peak in its interior on
each criterion, with the uninformative tails visible at each end. Binary
peaks in the interior too. As the one-parameter stay/move model described
in @sec-cost-metrics, its only lever is the aggregate stay/move split, so
its peak sits at the $\varepsilon$ where the diffusion of mass off the
diagonal matches the empirical move rate, and it peaks earlier than skill
and hierarchy, which keep improving as falling $\varepsilon$ sharpens an
off-diagonal allocation that pays off.
 
For KL the peak is more than a convenient scale-free summary. Since the
EROT plan is a multinomial-logit equilibrium and $\Delta KL$ is monotone in
the maximised log-likelihood, maximising $\Delta KL$ over the grid profiles
the likelihood over $\varepsilon$, the single unidentified scale parameter.
Peak $\Delta KL$ is therefore the profile-likelihood model-selection
criterion, and comparing peaks across metrics compares maximised
likelihoods. Peak $\Delta CWTVD$ carries no such derivation. CWTVD has no
likelihood for the peak to profile, so taking its maximum is the same
scale-free summary applied by analogy to KL, not an operation a
nuisance-parameter argument singles out: other scale-free summaries of the
$\Delta CWTVD$ curve would serve equally on that argument alone. What
licenses the peak for CWTVD is instead the resolving-power property
established in @sec-AC, that the peak $\Delta CWTVD$ gap between correlated
geometries tracks the true mixture more sharply than the KL gap does. The
justification for peaking CWTVD is thus empirical, resting on the
simulation that grounds the CWTVD case generally, where the justification
for peaking KL is analytic. We adopt the peak for both, holding them
co-equal, while noting the asymmetry in what each peak rests on.
 
The winner of the race is the cost matrix whose peak exceeds the nearest
rival's by at least 10\% on every criterion at once: peak $\Delta KL$, and
peak $\Delta CWTVD$ under each of the two informative judges. Requiring all
three is more selective than crowning the leader on any alone. A metric
wins only if the likelihood endorses its fit and the geometry-aware
criterion certifies it sound at both extremes of the blend family, so a
plan that puts mass in roughly the right cells but at the wrong distances,
scoring high on $\Delta KL$ and low on either geometric criterion, does not
win. Because the nearest rival can differ between the two judges, a winner
must lead whichever rival is closest under each. Three outcomes follow, and
we report whichever obtains:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Decisive win.} One metric leads the nearest rival by 10\%
  on all three criteria. The race resolves in its favour.
  \item \textbf{Endpoint split.} The two geometric criteria favour
  different metrics: one leads under $C_{\text{skill}}$-scoring, another
  under $C_{\text{hierarchy}}$-scoring. The winner is blend-dependent.
  Rather than a defect this is the design's most informative outcome, since
  a single blended judge would have crowned whichever metric led at the
  midpoint and concealed that the endpoints disagree. We report both, and
  the disagreement locates the mobility geometry of that regime as
  genuinely intermediate between the two rather than governed by either
  alone.
  \item \textbf{Unresolved.} No metric clears 10\% on all three criteria
  and the two geometric criteria do not cleanly favour different metrics.
  This covers both the case where the likelihood and geometry-aware
  criteria disagree about a single winner and the case where no candidate
  leads by 10\% on any criterion. We report which criteria favour which
  metric, since even an unresolved race describes how observed mobility
  departs from each candidate, but we name no governor.
\end{enumerate}
 
The 10\% threshold is an effect-size floor, set in advance and applied
uniformly to all three criteria. We treat two peak improvements differing
by less than ten percentage points as substantively equivalent regardless
of whether the difference is statistically distinguishable, on the grounds
that a smaller difference does not warrant naming one geometry the governor
of mobility in that regime. The floor is substantive, not statistical, so
it does not flex with the number of criteria: a gap below 10\% on a
geometric criterion is substantively unimpressive whether it stands alone
or beside the others, and correcting the bar for the count of criteria
would confuse an effect-size floor with a significance threshold. At the
sample sizes the linked census file provides, even the smallest sub-regime
holds thousands of transitions, so sampling noise in each peak gap is well
below this floor and the binding constraint is the substantive one. The one
regime where this could fail is the high-OES Binary sub-regime, whose low
mobility leaves its off-diagonal cells sparse. We therefore confirm at
access, by simulating a balanced skill/hierarchy mixture at that regime's
transition count, that a balanced mixture rarely produces a peak gap above
10\% on either geometric criterion; if it does, the Binary regime's race is
noise-limited and we interpret it as such.
 
An unresolved race is an informative no-decision rather than a coin to be
flipped. A disagreement between the likelihood-grounded and the
geometry-aware criteria, or between the two geometric endpoints, localizes
how a metric misfits, and breaking it by fiat would discard exactly the
signal the criteria were chosen to expose.

### Out-of-Regime Falsification {#sec-local-falsification}


The falsification scores $\Delta CWTVD$ under a single neutral cost matrix
rather than under the two informative judges used to adjudicate the race.
That matrix is $C$, the arithmetic mean of the three normalized cost
matrices $C_{\text{skill}}$, $C_{\text{hierarchy}}$, and
$C_{\text{binary}}$, in which no candidate geometry is privileged. The race
needs two judges because it resolves a close comparative contest between
correlated geometries, and bracketing the blend family is what certifies a
winner across it. The falsification needs the opposite: not a comparison
but a single fixed line that a predicted metric either crosses or does not.
A neutral blend supplies exactly one such line, and scoring the crossing
under two judges instead would reintroduce the grey zone the fixed line is
meant to remove. This is the one role for which the blend, retired from
adjudication, remains the right instrument.

The out-of-regime criterion is stated against independence, on this
neutral geometry-aware measure. In regime, the predicted winning metric,
$C_{\mathrm{skill}}$ in the Skill sub-regime and $C_{\mathrm{hierarchy}}$
in the Hierarchy sub-regime, peaks above independence on $\Delta KL$
and on $\Delta CWTVD$ under the neutral blend, since its geometry
rationalizes the transitions and improvement over independence is what the
horse race measures. Out of regime, where a new highest attainment resets
the worker's position and renders the 2016 occupation uninformative, that
metric is predicted to fall below independence on $\Delta CWTVD$.
 
The out-of-regime criterion rests on $\Delta CWTVD$ alone, and the reason
is that $\Delta KL$ cannot register the failure being tested. The
falsification asks whether the predicted metric has made the wrong
geometric bet, placing mass at the wrong distances. $\Delta CWTVD$ weights
each misallocation by distance and so penalises exactly this, falling below
independence when a short-move metric meets a movement-heavy matrix.
$\Delta KL$ is blind to geometry and scores any plan that captures the
diagonal stay/move structure, which every metric shares. A wrong-geometry
metric therefore collects partial KL credit for the diagonal even while its
off-diagonal bet is wrong, and its peak $\Delta KL$ can sit slightly above
independence rather than below it. This is visible in the simulations: in
the [online companion](https://rpmartin.github.io/not-one-thing-companion), under a binary data-generating process the skill and
hierarchy metrics peak below independence on $\Delta CWTVD$ but rise to a
small positive peak on $\Delta KL$ at moderate $\varepsilon$. Requiring the
geometry-blind measure to confirm a geometric failure would ask the wrong
instrument to register it. We therefore state the out-of-regime criterion
on $\Delta CWTVD$, the measure built to see what the falsification is about.
 
Setting the line at independence rather than at binary discharges the
conditionality that a binary benchmark would leave open. A wrongly
predicting metric always sits below binary out of regime, but whether its
$\Delta CWTVD$ also falls below independence depends on the non-local
transition matrix being movement-heavy: only when most credential-changers
move, and move far, does a short-move metric place enough mass on vacated
near pairs to fit worse than independence. We predict the non-local matrix
is movement-heavy, because the wormhole mechanism is precisely the claim
that a new credential drives long discontinuous jumps. The
below-independence criterion therefore tests two things at once. Its
crossing requires both that the predicted metric makes the wrong geometric
bet out of regime and that the non-local matrix is movement-heavy as the
mechanism predicts, so a metric whose $\Delta CWTVD$ falls below zero
jointly falsifies the local model out of regime and confirms the long-jump
prediction. A metric that stayed above independence out of regime would
either be governing where it should not or would reveal a non-local matrix
lighter than the mechanism requires, and either reading counts against the
design.
 
Independence is a fixed point, so the criterion is unambiguous. The
predicted metric's $\Delta CWTVD$ peak is either below zero or it is not,
with no margin to calibrate and no grey zone to adjudicate. This is the
respect in which the falsification differs from the race. The race resolves
a close contest between two correlated geometries by asking whether one
peak exceeds the other by 10\%, a margin set because the contestants are
near. The falsification asks whether a single metric crosses a fixed line,
which it either does or does not.
 
Peaking above independence in regime is a weaker bar than winning the
race, and the gap between them is real. A metric clears the in-regime side
of the falsification by improving on independence at all; it wins the race
only by leading every rival by 10\% on both measures. Both skill and
hierarchy peak well above independence in either of their sub-regimes,
since they are correlated and each partially rationalizes the other's
transitions, yet only one wins. Improving on independence is necessary for
a geometry to be governing at all; leading by 10\% on both measures is what
crowns it.
 
The mechanism that drives the predicted metric's $\Delta CWTVD$ below
independence is the same one that makes binary a useful point of
comparison. All three cost matrices assign zero self-distance,
$C_{ii} = 0$, so all three concentrate mass on the diagonal and capture the
dominant stay/move feature of the transition matrix. That diagonal
contribution is common to every plan, and what distinguishes the metrics is
the off-diagonal allocation. Binary makes no off-diagonal bet, since every
switch is equidistant under it, so it cannot be wrong about where movers
go. Skill and hierarchy do make that bet, and out of regime it is the wrong
one, because they place mass on geometrically proximate pairs that wormhole
movers avoid while the data concentrates on far pairs. A metric predicting
short moves into a movement-heavy matrix withholds mass from exactly where
the data sits, and $\Delta CWTVD$ penalises that misallocation by distance,
driving it below independence. The signature of this failure on
$\Delta CWTVD$ is a curve that rises monotonically toward the independence
baseline from below without crossing it, improving as $\varepsilon$ grows
only because diffusion toward independence is the one thing that helps a
metric whose geometry points the wrong way. The [online companion](https://rpmartin.github.io/not-one-thing-companion) shows this
under a binary data-generating process, where skill and hierarchy stay
below zero on $\Delta CWTVD$ across the grid while their $\Delta KL$, for
the diagonal-credit reason given above, rises instead to a small positive
peak at moderate $\varepsilon$, which is why the out-of-regime criterion
rests on $\Delta CWTVD$ rather than on both measures.
 
The sub-regime models are falsified the same way, with one exception. In
regime each sub-regime is expected to produce a metric that peaks above
independence on both measures, and out of regime that metric's $\Delta
CWTVD$ peak is predicted to fall below independence. We apply this to the
Skill and Hierarchy sub-regimes only. The Binary sub-regime is exempt from
the distance-based out-of-regime test for a reason internal to its own
hypothesis, and the exemption does not depend on what its out-of-regime
cell turns out to contain. Its in-regime claim is that no distance geometry
governs, so it never generates a prediction that distance ceases to govern
out of regime; there is no distance bet to be caught making wrongly, with
or without movers in the cell. Separately, the lock-in mechanism that
defines the sub-regime predicts that cell is near-empty, because workers
already in a high-OES occupation rarely acquire a new highest attainment,
since occupation-specific human capital is reached through a single
credentialing pipeline and confers no incentive to re-credential. A
non-empty cell therefore falsifies the lock-in premise without thereby
reinstating a distance test the hypothesis never licensed: the
distance-based leg stays inapplicable, and the non-emptiness is read as
evidence against lock-in in its own right. The out-of-regime content of the Binary hypothesis otherwise lies on the
entry side and is carried by the destination-OES coefficient in the
non-local specificity regression rather than by a horse race.

## Non-Local Model {#sec-non_local}

The non-local model estimates the conditional-on-positive relationship between how far a worker travels through occupation space and the pipeline strength of their transition, measured by lift. We measure that distance two ways, with different estimators and complementary roles. The primary outcome is $\log(d_{ij})$, the log skill distance between 2016 and 2021 occupations, estimated by OLS. The second is a binary indicator for whether the move crosses an occupation broad group, a silo, estimated by a linear probability model (LPM). The hierarchical metric is ordinal, not cardinal: its values, one through the cross-category sentinel of nine, are ranks with an assigned spacing rather than real distances, so they cannot enter an OLS outcome as a graded distance. Its distribution is also dominated by the cross-category sentinel, with within-silo values a thin minority, so the one contrast with mass on both sides is whether a move crosses a silo at all. The binary cross-silo indicator is therefore the operational form the metric supports for non-local jumps.

The cross-silo margin is the right hierarchical form because of where high-lift destinations sit. A high-lift move is by construction a move into a credential-fed occupation, and credential-fed occupations are concentrated in the skilled silos rather than in the generic entry silos such as sales and service, which contain few. The high-lift destinations within sales and service are a small and specific set of licensed or skilled-service occupations, funeral directors, chefs, insurance and real-estate agents, each fed by a dedicated credential, while the generic occupations that make up most of the silo are reached at close to baseline prevalence from every education. A high-lift credential earned by a worker in the generic part of such a silo therefore has almost no within-silo destination to channel into, so the move it opens is cross-silo by the structure of where credentials lead rather than by the length of the jump.

The mechanism is directional: a wormhole is a path a credential opens through occupation space. A specific education channels workers toward a narrow set of occupations that would otherwise be unreachable, and the long jump occurs when a worker travels along that channel into the occupation the credential distinctively feeds. This is a property of the education--destination pair, not of either alone, and one quantity measures it: the lift $m(e,n) = P(n\mid e)/P(n)$ of the destination occupation $n$ for the worker's education $e$, defined in @sec-cf as the cell-level term of the education-side specificity divergence. Read directly rather than aggregated, it makes the conjunction requirement automatic: a generic education offers no high-lift path to take, and a specific credential whose holder lands off its distinctive path realizes low lift wherever else they go, so only travel along a genuine pipeline registers as high. There is no need to build the conjunction from separate entrance and exit measures and no interaction term to specify; the pairing that a wormhole requires is exactly what lift measures.

This directness disposes of two cases that the separate-measures approach had to handle by construction. A worker who reaches a specific destination without the credential that feeds it arrives on general human capital, and lift reads their education--destination pair as low: the destination's specificity does not make it a wormhole for them, because their education does not lead there. And ability-driven search failure is handled the same way: two graduates with the same credential need not fare alike, one reaching the specific destination the credential opens and another, after a harder search, settling for a generic occupation nearby; the second has low destination lift and is correctly read as a short, non-pipeline move, entering the regression at its observed short distance rather than requiring a separate exclusion. The same low destination lift marks a relabelled or credential-unrelated move for reclassification to local under the wedge of @sec-rp, so the non-local regression and the wedge reclassification key on one quantity.

Let $y_{ij}$ denote the outcome ($\log(d_{ij})$ in skill space, estimated by OLS, or the cross-silo indicator, estimated by LPM), and let $\bar{d}_j$ be the destination's mean inbound distance under the independence baseline (its average distance from a randomly drawn origin; for the cross-silo outcome, the baseline probability that a random origin lies outside $j$'s broad group). The remoteness control is defined in the same space as the outcome it accompanies, so it swaps with the outcome: skill-space mean inbound distance for the OLS specification, baseline cross-silo probability for the LPM.

\begin{equation}
y_{ij} = \alpha + \beta\, \log(m(e_i, j)) + \gamma\bar{d}_j + \delta_i + \varepsilon_{ij}
\label{eq-lift}
\end{equation}

The specification includes origin occupation fixed effects $\delta_i$ and a destination remoteness control $\bar{d}_j$, but not destination fixed effects. The reason is structural, not one of feasibility. Lift is a property of the education--destination pair, so all workers who reach a given destination through the same education carry the identical lift; within a strong pipeline, where a destination is reached predominantly through one education, lift is very nearly constant, and the variation in distance among those workers comes from their differing origins, not from lift. Destination fixed effects would therefore identify the lift coefficient only from within-destination variation in lift, which is precisely what a pipeline lacks: the more exclusive the pipeline, the less within-destination lift variation it has, so destination fixed effects are blindest exactly where the mechanism is strongest. The identifying variation is between destinations, high-lift pipelines against low-lift ones, which is also what the wormhole claim is about. The remoteness control preserves that variation while netting out the one confound of concern, a destination lying far from all others in skill space, or in a small broad group most origins fall outside, which registers long jumps mechanically with no credential mechanism involved. Conditioning on $\bar{d}_j$ ensures the lift coefficient reflects credential-gated channeling rather than baseline remoteness; this is the conservative reading, since if remoteness is itself part of how specificity operates, the control absorbs some of the mechanism. Origin remoteness needs no separate term; $\delta_i$ absorbs it with every other origin-level determinant of distance.

Both outcome specifications share the lift coefficient $\beta$, expected to be positive: travel along a stronger education--occupation pipeline is longer, and more likely to cross a silo, since the pipeline is what carries a worker to a distant occupation the credential distinctively opens. The two coefficients read on a common per-1\%-of-lift basis, differing only in the units of their response. For the OLS skill-distance outcome, a 1\% increase in lift is associated with approximately a $\beta$ percent increase in distance, the log--log coefficient reading as an elasticity. For the cross-silo LPM, the same 1\% increase is associated with approximately a $\beta/100$ percentage-point increase in the probability of crossing a silo, the raw per-log-unit coefficient divided by 100 to convert it to a per-1\% effect. The remoteness coefficient $\gamma$ is expected to be positive. Standard errors will be clustered on education and destination occupation.

Age is excluded from the specification. The well-documented decline in occupational mobility with age [@topel1992job] is, for jump distance, a life-cycle composition effect that operates through the 2016 origin occupation: workers who acquire a new attainment later in life tend to start from a higher skill and hierarchy position than those completing the same credential early, so they sit closer to the credential's destination and travel a shorter measured distance. That channel is a property of where a worker starts, not of the wormhole mechanism, and the origin fixed effects $\delta_i$ absorb it along with every other origin-level determinant of distance. A separate age term is therefore neither needed nor clean: conditional on origin it carries no signal the mechanism predicts, and because age plausibly correlates with lift through selection into particular credential types, including it risks partialling out legitimate pipeline variation.

The model is evaluated across four samples as described in @sec-data, with results reported for both the skill and cross-silo outcomes. The within-$R^2$, the share of variance in the outcome explained by lift after partialling out origin fixed effects and destination remoteness, is not expected to be large in absolute terms: transition distance is inherently noisy and lift is an aggregate measure that captures only the systematic component of specificity-driven mobility. The relevant comparison is the ordering of within-$R^2$ across samples, not its absolute level.

The positive-distance restriction removes many apprenticeship completers, since NOC makes no distinction between apprentices and journeypeople of the same occupation: those already working in the target trade in 2016 show zero measured distance upon completion and are excluded by construction. Rather than threatening identification, this restriction improves measurement validity: the excluded zeros reflect occupation coarseness rather than true immobility, and their inclusion would introduce noise into the outcome variable. Workers who complete an entire apprenticeship program within the five-year window from a different 2016 occupation remain in the sample, and for these workers the wormhole mechanism is cleanly observable. The limitation is one of external validity rather than internal validity: estimates do not generalise to within-trade apprenticeship completers, whose human capital increment is real but invisible to NOC.

Beyond the apprenticeship case, the positive-distance restriction is also a selection on the outcome, but most of what it excludes is genuine immobility rather than a selection artifact. A true stayer contributes no distance to explain, so excluding stayers sets the scope of the conditional-on-positive estimand rather than selecting the surviving movers on anything, and the external-validity caveat above already covers it. The internal-validity concern is confined to the residual coarseness zeros, the real moves NOC records as zero distance, because OES predicts how often those occur as well as the distance conditional on moving. Insofar as the excluded zeros reflect coarseness rather than genuine immobility, the surviving positive subsample is selected on a margin the regressor also drives, with high-OES origins contributing their movers as a selected upper tail that the destination-side remoteness control does not absorb. The likely direction of that residual bias is attenuation, on the same logic as the local-sample leakage: the coarseness zeros are short measured moves, so resolving the coarseness would restore short high-OES moves that flatten the estimated specificity--distance gradient rather than steepen it. We therefore read the restricted estimate as attenuated, consistent with the lower-bound interpretation applied to the truncation in the limitations, and report it as such rather than as an unbiased effect.




### Out-of-Regime Falsification {#sec-non_local_false}

The non-local model is falsified in the local clean sample, where the highest
education attainment is unchanged. The criterion is the cross-sample degradation of the lift coefficient and the within-$R^2$, not their vanishing in absolute terms. Because lift enters on a common natural-log scale in every subsample, the $\beta$ estimate and the within-$R^2$ are directly comparable across subsamples, and the prediction is that both collapse from the non-local to the local sample. We do not require the local coefficient to be exactly zero: a high-lift education can compress local move distances weakly even absent a new credential, so the claim is degradation toward zero relative to the non-local estimate, consistent with the ordering-not-level standard applied to the within-$R^2$ throughout.

The collapse has two sources, and both are consistent with the wormhole
mechanism. Without a new highest attainment the wormhole channel is shut: the
worker's education is already reflected in their 2016 occupation, the starting
point of any local move, so it carries no additional predictive content for that
move, whereas the non-local education is acquired within the window and does its
repositioning where it can be observed. Second, high-lift transitions require a
worker to have moved into the occupation their credential distinctively feeds,
which without a new attainment is largely already reflected in the 2016
occupation, so high-lift realisations are truncated in the local sample and a
near-zero lift coefficient there reflects range restriction as much as a
switched-off mechanism. Neither reading threatens the falsification. A
spurious lift--distance relationship, one driven by a confound rather than
by credential-contingent enablement, would appear in both samples, since the
confound would not know which workers had changed education; its appearance in
neither the local coefficient nor anywhere a confound could hide is what marks
the relationship as credential-contingent rather than mechanical.

Two features of the local sample bear on its standing as a falsification sample.
It is large (most workers do not acquire a new highest attainment over the
inter-census period), so the null it delivers is precise rather than
underpowered, a well-powered absence of relationship rather than silence. It is
also subject to a modest contamination, because the partition variable is only a
proxy for the mechanism: what matters is whether the 2016 occupation is
informative, and "no substantial inter-census change in attainment" stands in for that.
Recorded highest attainment is in turn a lossy proxy for
the worker's actual position in human-capital space: any increment the record
fails to capture routes a genuinely repositioned worker into the local sample.
The failure takes several forms. A worker may earn a credential that does not
raise highest attainment, a sub-baccalaureate certificate, or a second field at
the same level, so that real training leaves the partition variable unmoved; a
nurse aide completing a practical-nursing certificate is one such case. Or the
timing may be wrong: a worker who earned their highest attainment shortly before
the 2016 reference week is formally local but holds a transitional rather than
credential-matched 2016 occupation, and so behaves like a non-local mover whose
jump straddles the census boundary. What unites these cases is not their cause
but their effect: the record misses a real increment, so the leakage cannot be
enumerated source by source, and the defense does not rest on cataloguing it.

The leakage is small, and the measurement-complete requirement removes one clear
class of it, excluding the graduates of intensive, occupationally specific programs, who
disproportionately lack a 2016 occupation at all. What matters more than any
filter is that whatever leakage remains biases toward the null, for a reason that
holds regardless of why the record failed: a leaked mover imports wormhole
behaviour into the local sample, degrading the horse-race fit and injecting
specificity into the regression, both of which work against the predicted
dissociation rather than producing it. This is the final reason the criterion is
stated as degradation and not as an absolute zero, which would be hostage to
precisely this contamination.

## Limitations

### Local Mobility

Two sample restriction mechanisms introduce a potential selection 
concern for local mobility. Non-linkage and non-observability of 
occupation are both disproportionately concentrated among 
low-attachment workers, individuals with casual, seasonal, or 
intermittent employment whose identifying information is also less 
stable across census cycles, so the two filters largely co-select 
the same low-skill population rather than introducing independent 
exclusions. This shared exclusion affects the representativeness of 
population-level transition estimates (external validity) but does not 
threaten the internal validity of the horse race. For the horse race
results to be biased, the excluded workers' transitions would need to be 
systematically more or less rationalizable by a particular cost 
matrix than those of their observed counterparts in the same region 
of occupational space. No such mechanism is apparent: exclusion is 
driven by attachment instability and identifier churn, neither of 
which has a clear relationship to how well transitions conform to 
any particular cost structure conditional on occupation. The residual 
unlinked population among otherwise-observable workers, recent 
immigrants, young workers, and high-movers, similarly lacks any 
obvious occupational-space concentration that would differentially 
favour or penalize a particular metric.

A notable omitted factor for local mobility  is \emph{path-specific} wage differentials. The additively separable component of wage gains, recoverable from origin and destination wage levels alone, is absorbed by the 
margins insofar as high-wage destinations attract larger inflows and 
low-wage origins larger outflows. The residual dyadic component, 
reflecting transition-specific wage premia and discounts beyond what 
origin and destination wage levels predict, is an omitted factor. 
Short-distance transitions are within a similar occupational 
neighbourhood, reducing employer uncertainty about candidate fit and 
productivity; long-distance transitions cross larger skill or 
hierarchical gaps, and employers may discount wage offers to 
compensate for that uncertainty, or workers may accept lower wages 
to gain entry to a distant occupation.

Thus, path-specific wage differentials are better understood as an 
alternative mechanism, rather than a confounder. If employers use the same metric that governs mobility to assess candidate fit uncertainty, discounting wages for transitions that are long under the winning metric, that discount reinforces worker selection toward shorter transitions under 
the same metric. Both channels predict identical patterns of 
transitions and are equally consistent with the winning metric being 
the correct description of the mobility geometry. The horse race 
identifies which distance geometry best rationalizes observed 
transitions in a reduced-form sense, but cannot separately attribute 
that rationalization to worker or employer preferences regarding 
distance.

### Non-Local Mobility

The non-local regime studies non-negative operative increments, as defined in @sec-rp: transitions where the operative credential rises above the worker's prior ceiling or respecifies at the same level. Substitutive moves, where an over-credentialed worker retrains below their ceiling and repositions on a sub-maximal credential, lie outside the estimand and are invisible to a highest-attainment record; the findings therefore speak to additive and lateral specific-human-capital activation, not to occupational mobility of every kind. This is a scope of the question rather than a gap in the answer, and it is consistent with the paper's premise that mobility is not one thing: the substitutive channel is a distinct phenomenon with its own economics, deserving its own treatment rather than absorption into this one.

The non-local partition is restricted to individuals who acquire a new highest educational attainment between 2016 and 2021 and report an occupation in both periods. A 2016 occupation is observed if and only if the individual was employed between May 1st and 7th, the 2016 census reference week. For the 2015/2016 school year, roughly half of 18-29 year old students reported concurrent work, with an (unweighted) ten percentage point decrease for university students, consistent with more intensive programs suppressing concurrent employment.^[source: Statistics Canada table 37-10-0104-01.] The Census reference week provides a partial offset: falling after the typical post-secondary academic year ends, it captures individuals who have recently finished exams and may have already begun summer employment. But this offset is weaker for intensive professional programs that are either year-round or have students for whom summer employment is atypical. The resulting truncation is not random: missingness is concentrated among the most occupationally specific educations, precisely the credentials that anchor the highest-lift pipelines, where the wormhole mechanism is strongest and jumps are longest. Thus estimates are attenuated toward zero and should be interpreted as lower bounds on the true relationship, given that truncation is concentrated precisely where the signal is strongest. Notably, this missingness pattern is not purely a limitation: the disproportionate absence of 2016 occupations among the most specific credentials is itself consistent with the wormhole mechanism, since program intensity and specificity are precisely what suppresses concurrent employment. In the online companion we plot each education's occupational specificity against the share of its workers missing a 2016 occupation, quantifying the magnitude of this truncation.

The specificity regression faces an analogous identification 
challenge to the horse race. Lift is observed and enters the 
regression, but cannot distinguish between two mechanisms that 
predict identical patterns. A specific education opens doors to 
particular distant occupations that a general education does not: 
the human capital match is narrow, so only a subset of distant 
destinations become reachable following attainment (enablement). At 
the same time, workers with specific educations may face stronger 
incentives to seek out distant occupations where those skills are 
scarce and rewarded, making long-distance moves financially attractive 
relative to staying within a crowded local neighbourhood (motivation). 
Because both channels operate through the same pipelines that lift 
measures, the reduced-form estimate conflates the two and cannot be separately 
attributed to either. The regression should therefore be interpreted 
as identifying the reduced-form predictive relationship between 
pipeline strength and distance traveled, without attribution to a specific 
mechanism, though the estimate remains informative: if either 
channel is operative, the regression will detect it.

## Conclusion

- What we found \[PLACEHOLDER: awaiting data\]

The central policy takeaway from this analysis is that labour market adjustment mechanisms are not one-size-fits-all: the appropriate intervention depends on which mobility regime contains the occupation experiencing a shortage. The three mobility sub-regimes suggest three distinct policy levers.

In the Skill sub-regime, reskilling and short-cycle training are the natural adjustment mechanisms. Workers in adjacent occupations already possess much of the relevant task content, and targeted reskilling can accelerate the reallocation of labour toward occupations in shortage without requiring formal retraining. The policy implication is that investment in modular, portable training that builds on existing skill profiles will generate the largest mobility response in this segment.

In the Hierarchy sub-regime, the relevant bottleneck is not skill transferability but the hierarchy's silo and platform structure. An occupational shortage within one silo cannot be addressed by upskilling workers from a different silo, even if the occupations share a near-identical skill profile. Instead, shortages must be addressed within-silo, through either lateral movement on a platform or vertical movement between platforms. The best way to address a shortage at a higher platform is by increasing the supply of workers to lower platforms, freeing incumbents to pursue upward movement through the silo, the occupational analogue of the internal labour market adjustment mechanism described by @doeringer1971internal. Bridging programs, mentorship structures, and targeted recruitment into within-silo entry-level positions are the appropriate instruments.

In the Binary sub-regime, either a worker has the required education, or they do not. Neither reskilling nor within-silo movement can substitute for education. Adjustment in this sub-regime depends entirely on expanding formal training pipelines: increasing capacity in the relevant educational programs, reducing barriers to program entry, and shortening time-to-completion where possible. These are also the occupations that immigration policy should target, both in terms of admission and rapid credential recognition. 

If the hypothesized sub-regime structure is confirmed, the geometry of occupational mobility determines which policy lever to pull, and the wrong lever is not just ineffective but potentially counterproductive.
